questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Indefinite Integral of a Rational Function Using Partial Fractions
questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\int \frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)}\,\text{d}x=a\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+b\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+6|+C,
$$

find the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)} & =\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+6},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
7=A(x+6)+B(x-1).
$$

Plugging in $x=-6,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7 & =A(-6+6)+B(-6-1) \\ 7 & =-7B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=1,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7 & =A(1+6)+B(1-1) \\ 7 & =7A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)} & =\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+6})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+6|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=1,b=-1,$ and $a+b=1-1=0.$

questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\int \frac{13}{(3x+2)(2x-3)}\,\text{d}x=a\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-3|+b\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+2|+C,
$$

find the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{(3x+2)(2x-3)} & =\frac{A}{3x+2}+\frac{B}{2x-3},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
13=A(2x-3)+B(3x+2).
$$

Plugging in $x=\frac{3}{2},$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}13 & =A(2(\frac{3}{2})-3)+B(3(\frac{3}{2})+2) \\ 13 & =\frac{13}{2}B \\ B & =2\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\frac{2}{3},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}13 & =A(2(-\frac{2}{3})-3)+B(3(-\frac{2}{3})+2) \\ 13 & =-\frac{13}{3}A \\ A & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{(3x+2)(2x-3)}=-\frac{3}{3x+2}+\frac{2}{2x-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{13}{(3x+2)(2x-3)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{3}{3x+2}+\frac{2}{2x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{3}{3x+2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{2}{2x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=1,b=-1,$ and $a+b=1-1=0.$

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)} & =\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-4},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
2x-4=A(x-4)+Bx.
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(4)-4 & =A(4-4)+B(4) \\ 4 & =4B \\ 1 & =B\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-4 & =A(0-4)+B(0) \\ -4 & =-4A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)} & =\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+7}{(2x+1)(x+2)} & =\frac{A}{2x+1}+\frac{B}{x+2},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
2x+7=A(x+2)+B(2x+1).
$$

Plugging in $x=-2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-2)+7 & =A((-2)+2)+B(2(-2)+1) \\ 3 & =-3B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-\frac{1}{2})+7 & =A(-\frac{1}{2}+2)+B(2(-\frac{1}{2})+1) \\ 6 & =A(\frac{3}{2}) \\ A & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+7}{(2x+1)(x+2)} & =\frac{4}{2x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+7}{(2x+1)(x+2)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{4}{2x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6x+12}{x(x+3)} & =\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x+3},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
6x+12=A(x+3)+Bx.
$$

Plugging in $x=-3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6(-3)+12 & =A(-3+3)+B(-3) \\ -6 & =-3B \\ B & =2\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6(0)+12 & =A(0+3)+B(0) \\ 12 & =3A \\ A & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6x+12}{x(x+3)}=\frac{4}{x}+\frac{2}{x+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6x+12}{x(x+3)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{4}{x}+\frac{2}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Partial Fractions
questions.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)} & =\frac{A}{(x-2)}+\frac{B}{(x+4)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
2x+2=A(x+4)+B(x-2).
$$

Plugging in $x=-4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-4)+2 & =A(-4+4)+B(-4-2) \\ -6 & =-6B \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2)+2 & =A(2+4)+B(2-2) \\ 6 & =6A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}=\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{x+4}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{x+4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-2)(x+4)|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-2)(x+4)|{|}_{3}^{6} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(40)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\  & =ln\,(\frac{40}{7}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that the denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
{x}^{2}-8x+12=(x-2)(x-6).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x+7}{{x}^{2}-8x+12} & =\frac{3x+7}{(x-2)(x-6)}=\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{B}{x-6},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
3x+7=A(x-6)+B(x-2).
$$

Plugging in $x=6,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(6)+7 & =A(6-6)+B(6-2) \\ 25 & =4B \\ B & =\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2)+7 & =A(2-6)+B(2-2) \\ 13 & =-4A \\ A & =-\frac{13}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{3x+7}{{x}^{2}-8x+12}=-\frac{13}{4(x-2)}+\frac{25}{4(x-6)}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+7}{{x}^{2}-8x+12}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{13}{4(x-2)}+\frac{25}{4(x-6)})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{13}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\frac{25}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-6|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+7}{{x}^{2}-8x+12}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{13}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\frac{25}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-6|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{5}\frac{3x+7}{{x}^{2}-8x+12}\,\text{d}x & ={[-\frac{13}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\frac{25}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-6|]}_{3}^{5} \\  & =(-\frac{13}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+\frac{25}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1))-(-\frac{13}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{25}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & =-\frac{13}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-\frac{25}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\  & =-\frac{19}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
5{x}^{2}-19x-4=(5x+1)(x-4).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{15x-39}{5{x}^{2}-19x-4} & =\frac{15x-39}{(5x+1)(x-4)}=\frac{A}{5x+1}+\frac{B}{x-4},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
15x-39=A(x-4)+B(5x+1).
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}15(4)-39 & =A(4-4)+B(5(4)+1) \\ 21 & =21B \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\frac{1}{5},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}15(-\frac{1}{5})-39 & =A(-\frac{1}{5}-4)+B(5(-\frac{1}{5})+1) \\ -42 & =-\frac{21}{5}A \\ A & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{15x-39}{5{x}^{2}-19x-4}=\frac{10}{5x+1}+\frac{1}{x-4}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{15x-39}{5{x}^{2}-19x-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{10}{5x+1}+\frac{1}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+1|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{15x-39}{5{x}^{2}-19x-4}\,\text{d}x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+1|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(5x+1)^{2}(x-4)|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{15x-39}{5{x}^{2}-19x-4}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(5x+1)^{2}(x-4)|{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(242)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{242}{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{121}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
5{x}^{2}+16x+3=(5x+1)(x+3).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3} & =\frac{14}{(5x+1)(x+3)}=\frac{A}{(5x+1)}+\frac{B}{(x+3)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
14=A(x+3)+B(5x+1).
$$

Plugging in $x=-3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & =A(-3+3)+B(5(-3)+1) \\ 14 & =-14B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\frac{1}{5},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & =A(-\frac{1}{5}+3)+B(5(-\frac{1}{5})+1) \\ 14 & =\frac{14}{5}A \\ A & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}=\frac{5}{5x+1}-\frac{1}{(x+3)}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{5}{5x+1}-\frac{1}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{5}{5x+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{5x+1}{x+3}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{11}\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{5x+1}{x+3}|{|}_{4}^{11} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}^{2}-16=(x+4)(x-4).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16} & =\frac{3x+4}{(x+4)(x-4)}=\frac{A}{(x+4)}+\frac{B}{(x-4)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
3x+4=A(x-4)+B(x+4).
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(4)+4 & =A(4-4)+B(4+4) \\ 16 & =8B \\ B & =2\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-4,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-4)+4 & =A(-4-4)+B(-4+4) \\ -8 & =-8A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16}=\frac{1}{(x+4)}+\frac{2}{(x-4)}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{(x+4)}+\frac{2}{(x-4)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-4)^{2}|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+4)(x-4)^{2}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{3x+4}{{x}^{2}-16}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+4)(x-4)^{2}|{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(24) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{24}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & =A(x+4)+B(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=-4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5(-4) & =A(-4+4)+B(-4-1) \\ -20 & =-5B \\ B & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, by plugging in $x=1,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5(1) & =A(1+4)+B(1-1) \\ 5 & =5A \\ A & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{5x}{x^2+3x-4}  = \dfrac{1}{(x-1)} +\dfrac{4}{(x+4)}.
$$

$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
4x^2-1 = (2x+1)(2x-1) \,.
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+3}{4{x}^{2}-1} & =\frac{2x+3}{(2x+1)(2x-1)} \\  & =\frac{A}{(2x+1)}+\frac{B}{(2x-1)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =A(2x-1)+B(2x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=\dfrac{1}{2},$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(\frac{1}{2})+3 & =A(2(\frac{1}{2})-1)+B(2(\frac{1}{2})+1) \\ 4 & =2B \\ B & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\dfrac{1}{2},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-\frac{1}{2})+3 & =A(2(-\frac{1}{2})-1)+B(2(-\frac{1}{2})+1) \\ 2 & =-2A \\ A & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{2x+3}{4x^2-1} = -\dfrac{1}{(2x+1)} +\dfrac{2}{(2x-1)}.
$$

Now, we integrate and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+3}{4{x}^{2}-1}\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{1}{(2x+1)}+\frac{2}{(2x-1)})\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{2x+1}\text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{2x-1}\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+2(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|)+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+3}{4{x}^{2}-1}\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{2x+3}{4{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{|\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{3})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7\sqrt{3}}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$
